entries.question: Walk through the front door of the home you remember best from childhood. What is the first thing you see, hear, and smell?
entries.answer: The green front door, first of all. It stuck every time it rained, so you had to put your shoulder to it and push until it gave. Inside it smelled of rice cooking and floor wax, and a little of the kerosene Papa kept by the lamp for when the power went out. Mama always had the radio on low in the kitchen, so you heard music before you heard anybody talking. Even now the smell of floor wax makes me want to take my shoes off at the door.
entries.page:
The front door of Rosa's childhood home was green, and when it rained it stuck. She put her shoulder to it and pushed until it gave.

Inside, the house smelled of rice cooking and floor wax, and a little of the kerosene Papa kept by the lamp for when the power went out.

Mama had the radio on low in the kitchen. Rosa heard music before she heard anybody talking.

Even now, the smell of floor wax makes her want to take her shoes off at the door.

entries.question: Where in that home did you feel safest? Describe the spot.
entries.answer: Under the stairs, where the brooms were kept. There was a gap at the back just big enough for me, and I kept a biscuit tin there with a blue ribbon tied around it. Inside were two marbles, one cloudy and one clear, and the only photograph I had of my grandmother, in a dress with a white collar. When the house got loud I crawled in with the tin on my knees and listened to the rain on the roof until things were quiet again. Nobody ever came looking for me there, and I think they always knew exactly where I was.
entries.page:
Under the stairs was where the brooms were kept. At the back there was a gap just big enough for Rosa.

She kept a biscuit tin there, with a blue ribbon tied around it. Inside were two marbles, one cloudy and one clear, and the only photograph she had of her grandmother, who wore a dress with a white collar.

When the house got loud, Rosa crawled in with the tin on her knees. She listened to the rain on the roof until things were quiet again.

Nobody ever came looking for her there. She thinks they always knew exactly where she was.

entries.question: Who else lived in that home? Pick one person and tell me about an ordinary day with them.
entries.answer: It was Mama, Papa, my little brother Nico and me, and I will pick Mama, because her days all had the same shape. She was up before everyone and back from the market with her basket before we were awake. Then came the washing, and all afternoon she ironed other people's shirts by the kitchen window, where the light was best. She sang along with the radio, but only when she thought nobody was listening, so I learned to sit very still in the next room. At supper she never sat down; she ate standing at the stove and called it resting.
entries.page:
Four people lived in the house: Mama, Papa, Rosa's little brother Nico, and Rosa.

Of the four, Rosa picks Mama, because her days all had the same shape.

Mama was up before everyone. She was back from the market with her basket before the children were awake. Then came the washing, and all afternoon she ironed other people's shirts by the kitchen window, where the light was best.

The radio was on low in the kitchen, and Mama sang along with it, but only when she thought nobody was listening. So Rosa learned to sit very still in the next room.

At supper Mama never sat down. She ate standing at the stove and called it resting.

entries.question: Tell me about a meal you remember from that home: who cooked, and who sat where.
entries.answer: Sunday lunch was the one meal we all sat down for. Mama cooked chicken stew with potatoes, and I was sent to the bakery on the corner for bread that was still warm when I got home. Papa sat at the head of the table, I sat on his left, and Nico sat across from me and kicked my shins under the oilcloth. Papa made grace extra long on purpose, because he knew how hungry we were, and gave thanks for the chicken, the potatoes, the bakery and every one of the neighbours. Mama would say his name once from the stove, and he would laugh and say amen.
entries.page:
Sunday lunch was the one meal they all sat down for.

Mama cooked chicken stew with potatoes. Rosa was sent to the bakery on the corner for bread, and she carried it home still warm.

Papa sat at the head of the table. Rosa sat on his left, and Nico sat across from her and kicked her shins under the oilcloth.

Papa made grace extra long on purpose, because he knew how hungry they were. He gave thanks for the chicken, the potatoes, the bakery and every one of the neighbours.

Mama would say his name once from the stove. He would laugh and say amen.

entries.question: Was there a place outside that home that felt like yours, like a tree, a step, or a corner of the street?
entries.answer: The steps of the bakery on the corner. There were three stone steps, worn smooth in the middle, and the bottom one was mine. In the afternoons I sat there with my chin on my knees and watched the street: the ice cart, the big girls coming home from the high school, the dogs who knew which doors to wait at. The baker's wife, Belen, never once told me to move along. Near closing she would come out wiping her hands on her apron and put a broken roll in my lap without a word.
entries.page:
Outside the house, there was a place that was Rosa's. It was the steps of the bakery on the corner, the same bakery she was sent to on Sundays for bread.

There were three stone steps, worn smooth in the middle, and the bottom one was hers. In the afternoons she sat there with her chin on her knees and watched the street: the ice cart, the big girls coming home from the high school, the dogs who knew which doors to wait at.

The baker's wife, Belen, never once told her to move along.

Near closing Belen would come out wiping her hands on her apron and put a broken roll in Rosa's lap without a word.

entries.question: What object from that home do you wish you still had?
entries.answer: The biscuit tin from under the stairs. We moved the year I turned twelve, somebody packed that space in a hurry, and the tin went into a box and the box went somewhere. I did not mind so much about the marbles or the ribbon. It was the photograph of my grandmother, Mama's mother, whom I never met, and it was the only picture of her I ever had. For years I looked inside every box Mama opened, and sometimes I still catch myself looking.
entries.page:
Rosa was twelve the year they moved. Somebody packed the space under the stairs in a hurry, and the biscuit tin went into a box, and the box went somewhere.

She did not mind so much about the marbles or the blue ribbon. It was the photograph she minded. Her grandmother, Mama's mother, in a dress with a white collar. Rosa never met her, and it was the only picture of her she ever had.

For years she looked inside every box Mama opened.

Sometimes she still catches herself looking.
